notes.meaning: The story happens in the time of the judges, before Israel had kings. A famine hit the land, even Bethlehem, whose name means "house of bread." Matthew Henry sees the famine as one of the warnings God had promised for Israel's sins. Elimelech cared for his family by taking them along, but the older writers think moving to Moab, a land of other gods, showed a lack of trust in God.

differ.view: The famine does not have to mean God was punishing Bethlehem; it only shows it was severe. God never banned looking for food abroad, and he once sent his own people to Egypt in a famine.

notes.meaning: The names carry meaning. Elimelech means "my God is king," and Naomi means "pleasant." Mahlon and Chilion sound like "sickness" and "wasting," so they may have been weak children who were not likely to live long. "Ephrathites" means people from Bethlehem, since Ephrath was the town's old name.
Elimelech died in Moab, probably not long after they arrived. Naomi was left with her two sons in a foreign land. Matthew Henry notes that wherever we go, we cannot run away from death.

The sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Ruth was Mahlon's wife. Many older writers think these marriages went against God's law, and the old Jewish paraphrase of the Bible says the same. Yet the Geneva Notes see God's wonderful providence here, meaning his care and rule over events. Through this marriage Ruth came into God's family, and Christ would one day come from her line.

differ.view: God's law banned marrying Canaanites, not Moabites. It only kept Moabites out of Israel's worshiping assembly, and the book itself never blames the sons.

notes.meaning: Both sons died too, and neither left children. Naomi lost her husband and her sons, so she was a widow with no one to care for her. Some older writers see the early deaths as God's judgment on the marriages. Matthew Henry says grief often comes wave after wave, and only God can truly comfort someone this low.

differ.view: The text shows no sign that God was angry. We should not assume these deaths were punishment, just as Jesus warned about the people killed by the tower of Siloam.

notes.meaning: Naomi heard that the LORD had "attended to" his people. That means he had turned his kindness back toward them and given them food again. She longed for life among God's people, so she got ready to go home. Matthew Henry says that once the reason for staying in a bad place is gone, we should not keep staying there.

Naomi set out for Judah, and both daughters-in-law went with her. Their company shows how much love there was between them. Matthew Henry says Naomi must have been kind to them and won their hearts, a good example for any mother-in-law.

Partway along, Naomi urged them to go back to their mothers' homes. Women and daughters often shared the same part of the house, and a mother could best comfort a grieving daughter. Naomi blessed them in the LORD's name. She asked him to show them loyal, faithful love, just as they had shown to their husbands and to her.

Naomi prayed that each would find "rest" with a new husband, meaning a settled, safe life free from a widow's troubles. Matthew Henry says a good marriage is a kind of rest and a gift from God, though only God is the soul's full rest. Then she kissed them goodbye, as people did when parting, and they all wept.

differ.view: Naomi had grown cool in faith from living among idol-worshipers, so she cared more about their bodily comfort than their souls.

notes.meaning: Both young women insisted they would go with Naomi to her people. Matthew Henry calls it rare love for a mother-in-law. But he notes that even Orpah, who later turned back, said this. Strong feelings without a settled mind often lead to weak promises.

Naomi points to an old custom. If a man died without children, his brother would marry the widow so the family line could go on. Naomi has no more sons to offer them. Wesley thinks she had already taught them this as part of Israel's faith.

Naomi says she is too old to remarry. Even if she married that very night and had sons, the young women could not wait for them to grow up. She feels "the hand of the LORD" has gone out against her, and she takes God's correction to herself. Some translate her words as "it is far more bitter for me than for you." The older writers say she wanted them to count the cost before choosing to follow Israel's God.

They wept again. Orpah kissed Naomi goodbye, but Ruth clung to her, the same word used of a husband holding fast to his wife in Genesis 2. Orpah loved Naomi, but not enough to leave her homeland. Matthew Henry and Wesley say many people are like that with Christ: they like him, yet leave him because they love other things more.

Naomi points out that Orpah has gone back to her people and her gods. The chief god of Moab was Chemosh. Naomi urges Ruth to follow her. Wesley and Matthew Henry see this as a test of Ruth's sincerity, and a hint that coming with Naomi meant taking up the true faith.

differ.view: Naomi was not testing Ruth. She sincerely wanted Ruth's earthly good, because her own trust in God had been shaken by her losses.

notes.meaning: Ruth begs Naomi to stop urging her to leave. She will go where Naomi goes and live where she lives. Naomi's people will be her people, and Naomi's God will be her God. In other words, she is leaving the gods of Moab behind. Matthew Henry calls it God's grace drawing her heart to choose what is best. It shows how anyone who turns to God also takes God's people as their own.

Ruth will even die and be buried where Naomi is, in hope that they would rise together one day. She seals it with a serious oath in the LORD's name, asking God to punish her if anything but death parts them. She kept her word, and later lived with Naomi in Boaz's house. Matthew Henry adds that our bond with Christ should hold even closer, since not even death can part us from him.

Naomi saw that Ruth's mind was made up, so she stopped arguing. Matthew Henry and Wesley see the power of a firm decision here. A half-made choice is like a door left open that invites a thief. A firm choice shuts and bolts the door.

The two women made the long trip to Bethlehem, at least 50 miles. The whole town was stirred, which shows Naomi's family had once been well known and respected. The women asked, "Can this be Naomi?" They were shocked at how grief and loss had changed her. Most likely they spoke with pity.

Naomi means "pleasant," but she asks to be called Mara, which means "bitter." She says the Almighty has dealt bitterly with her. The name "Almighty" can mean the One who is all-sufficient. Matthew Henry sees humble patience here: she accepts that her trouble came from God's hand and does not pretend things are fine.

differ.view: Naomi forgot her own part in what happened and seemed to blame the Almighty.

notes.meaning: Naomi left "full," with a husband, two sons and their goods, and she came back "empty." She says the LORD has "testified against" her, a courtroom picture of God giving a sentence. Matthew Henry reminds us that there is a deeper fullness in God that can never be taken away.

Naomi returned with Ruth, called "the Moabitess" to remind us she was an outsider. They arrived as the barley harvest began, in early spring around Passover. The timing was just right, because it sets up Ruth's gleaning in the next chapter. Matthew Henry notes that God holds both the events of our lives and their timing.
